title: First New Sea Spider Species in 100 Years Discovered in Salish Sea
summary:
If you imagine tiny hairy legs crawling up your body while swimming at night, there's now a real reason that image feels possible. Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified two previously unknown sea spider species in the Salish Sea — the first new ones formally described there in nearly 100 years.

Sea spiders aren't actually spiders. They belong to an ancient lineage that arose roughly 500 million years ago, related to spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs. But unlike their land relatives, they stayed entirely marine. Their biology is bizarre: some have up to 12 legs, they breathe directly through their skin, and males carry and raise the young. Females have ovaries that extend through their limbs, where eggs develop before popping out through a dedicated pore. During mating, the male collects eggs using specialized appendages near his head called "ovigers," coats them with glue from his legs, and attaches the egg clusters to his own body.

One new species, Callipallene pilosuspedes, is named for the Latin words for "hairy feet" because of the long, curved spines on its lower legs. It has red eyes and a short proboscis (a sucking tube) equipped with claws for grabbing food. Its mouth is triangular, divided into three lips, and surrounded by sensory tendrils — giving it an appearance reminiscent of a tiny marine Sarlacc pit. Under a microscope, researchers watched it wrap its agile ovigers around its legs and use comb-like spines to groom itself. Despite its memorable appearance, the team found only a single specimen.

The second species, Tanystylum kiixin (pronounced "kee-hin"), takes its name from an ancient Indigenous village site near where it was collected. The name refers to the sound of waves crashing at the base of that site. Unlike Callipallene pilosuspedes, this species has much smaller and less flexible egg-carrying limbs, which limits its ability to groom itself effectively.

The discoveries, published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, combine physical observations with genetic analysis. According to researcher Toler-Scott, this matters because "in order to understand how marine invertebrates are being impacted by things like climate change and how we can better protect these key elements of the ecosystem, we have to be able to identify them."
why_it_matters: Naming a species is the first step in protecting it: without names and genetic data, scientists cannot track how warming seas, pollution or climate change are reshaping the small invertebrates that hold marine food webs together — and those changes eventually reach the fish people eat.

background_read: Sea spiders are not true spiders: they are 'pycnogonids', an ancient group of marine arthropods (animals with jointed legs and hard outer shells) whose lineage split from the ancestors of spiders, scorpions and horseshoe crabs roughly 500 million years ago — long before dinosaurs or sharks existed.

The Salish Sea (the cold coastal waters between Vancouver Island in Canada and Washington State in the U.S.) is one of the most closely studied marine regions on Earth, yet small creatures living there can still go unnoticed for a century.

The work was led by the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada, which runs one of the country's largest natural-history collections, and the findings appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Organisms Diversity & Evolution.

New species names often honour a place or a people, which is why Tanystylum kiixin refers to kiixin, an ancient Indigenous village site on the west coast of Vancouver Island in the traditional territory of the Huu-ay-aht First Nations.
The 'Sarlacc pit' comparison comes from Star Wars — a fictional desert pit with a toothy mouth — chosen because the new sea spider's three-lipped mouth looks remarkably like one.

perspectives.description: After nearly a century without a new sea spider description in this region, two species turned up at once, showing that even well-studied waters still hide undiscovered life. The naming of Tanystylum kiixin after an Indigenous village site also links scientific discovery to local culture and history.

One of the species is known from a single specimen, which makes it hard to tell whether it is genuinely rare or simply easy to miss. Describing a species from such limited material can leave questions about how it varies and where else it lives.

The roughly 100-year gap is less about the animals disappearing than about how few specialists study sea spiders and how slowly taxonomy — the science of naming and classifying life — is funded. Museum collections and DNA analysis are now making hidden species easier to spot.

Genetic tools plus more sampling in cold, deep or poorly surveyed waters could reveal many more unknown invertebrates in the coming years. The next question is whether protection rules can keep up with discoveries in a sea shared by two countries and busy shipping lanes.
